title: Real Numbers — Chapter Summary
intro: Real numbers include the natural numbers, integers, rationals and irrationals you've already met. This chapter sharpens that view using two big ideas — Euclid's division lemma (and the algorithm built on it) and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. We use these to find HCF and LCM efficiently, prove that √2 is irrational, and decide when a rational has a terminating decimal.

branches.label: Fundamental theorem
details: HCF: smallest powers of common primes
LCM: largest powers of all primes

branches.label: HCF × LCM = a × b
details: Find one if other three known

sections.heading: Euclid's Division Lemma and Algorithm
bullets: Lemma: For positive integers a, b there exist UNIQUE integers q, r with a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r < b.
Algorithm to find HCF(a, b): apply lemma to (a, b), then to (b, r₁), then to (r₁, r₂), …
The remainders strictly decrease, so the process terminates.
The LAST NON-ZERO remainder is the HCF.

sections.heading: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
bullets: Every composite number has a UNIQUE prime factorisation (up to order).
HCF: take the SMALLEST power of each prime appearing in BOTH factorisations.
LCM: take the LARGEST power of every prime appearing in EITHER.
Always: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b.
Generalises to three or more numbers (use min/max powers across all).

sections.heading: Irrational Numbers
bullets: Rational: can be written p/q with q ≠ 0; irrational: cannot.
Famous irrationals: √2, √3, √5, π, e.
Theorem: √2 is irrational. Proof by contradiction: if √2 = p/q in lowest terms then p² = 2q² → p even → q even, contradicting lowest-terms.
Same idea proves √3, √5, √7 irrational.
Rational + irrational = irrational; non-zero rational × irrational = irrational.
But irrational × irrational CAN be rational (e.g., √2 × √2 = 2).

sections.heading: Decimal Expansions of Rationals
bullets: Every rational has either a terminating decimal OR a non-terminating REPEATING decimal.
Theorem: p/q in lowest terms has a TERMINATING decimal if and only if q is of the form 2^m · 5^n.
Otherwise, p/q has a non-terminating repeating decimal.
Number of digits after the decimal point in a terminating expansion = max(m, n).
Non-terminating: 23/30 = 23/(2·3·5) — has a 3 → repeating.

key_takeaways: Euclid's lemma: a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b.
Euclid's algorithm: last non-zero remainder = HCF.
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: unique prime factorisation.
HCF (min powers) × LCM (max powers) = a × b.
√2, √3, √5, π are irrational; proof by contradiction.
Rational ± irrational = irrational; non-zero rational × irrational = irrational.
Rational p/q (lowest terms) terminates ↔ q is 2^m · 5^n.

glossary.definition: All rational and irrational numbers; includes integers, fractions, decimals, surds.
For positive integers a, b: a = bq + r with unique q and 0 ≤ r < b.
A method to find HCF by repeated application of the lemma; the last non-zero remainder is the HCF.
Every composite number has a unique prime factorisation (up to order).
The largest positive integer that divides each of the given integers.
The smallest positive integer divisible by each of the given integers.
A number that can be written as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0.
A real number that cannot be written as p/q; its decimal is non-terminating, non-repeating.
A decimal expansion with a finite number of digits.
A decimal that goes on forever but in which a fixed group of digits repeats.
An irrational n-th root of a number, e.g., √2.
An integer greater than 1 with no positive divisors other than 1 and itself.
A method of proof: assume the opposite of what you want to prove, derive a contradiction, conclude.
